structure.title: Book I · An education made of people
structure.text: Marcus opens by assigning credit. A grandfather's temper, a teacher's plain living and a ruler's patience supply the details of a good life before Marcus has offered a single argument for it.

structure.title: Books II–XII · Return to the scene of the difficulty
structure.text: The remaining books move among mornings, irritations, illness, praise and death. An insight about other people in one entry may have to be worked out all over again the next time someone is ungrateful. The repetitions preserve how much practice that costs.

people.name: Marcus addressing Marcus
people.role: The voice on both sides of an argument
people.text: A second-person command can sound severe until you remember who will have to obey it. Marcus gives himself excuses, diagnoses their appeal and occasionally writes the answer he would like to have ready tomorrow.

people.name: Antoninus Pius
people.text: Marcus remembers a man who could sit through a long investigation and let somebody else take credit. Such recollections put a day's administrative choices beside the more imposing claims the book makes about virtue.

people.name: Rusticus
people.role: The teacher who lent Marcus a book
people.text: In the first book Marcus thanks Rusticus for lending him his copy of the writings of Epictetus. He remembers other lessons from the same man, among them how to read carefully and how to be reconciled with someone after a quarrel. The name of a philosopher comes attached to a memory of how an older man behaved.

context.title: An impression and what you add
context.text: A colleague may actually have spoken rudely. Marcus asks how much of his distress comes from a further judgment about insult, injury or status. Separating those steps gives him something to do while the colleague remains difficult.

context.title: Why Marcus keeps starting over
context.text: An argument addressed to another person can stop once that person agrees. Marcus often addresses the version of himself who will soon be tired or irritated again. Repetition can therefore tell us something a single polished statement could conceal, including which of his own convictions he found hardest to keep hold of during a working day.

notice.text: Watch a luxury get taken apart.
notice.why: Marcus describes costly things by their physical ingredients. Momentarily seeing coloured cloth or a dead fish where a dinner guest sees distinction is an exercise in loosening the thing's hold.

notice.text: Follow him back to other people.
notice.why: A view from high above can make today's quarrel look absurdly small. Marcus still has to go downstairs and work with the person who annoyed him. His insistence on human cooperation gives that change of scale a destination.

passages.quote: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody

notice.text: Hear the objection from under the bedclothes.
notice.why: Marcus has told himself to get up and do the work of a human being. The next voice in the argument points out that staying warm is pleasanter. He gives that voice only a few words, but allows it to state the difficulty exactly. A principle he accepts while writing has to defeat a very comfortable bed when morning comes.

passages.quote: to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm

opening: Marcus Aurelius commanded an empire, but he still had to talk himself into getting out of bed. Stoic philosophy gave him arguments for doing his work, enduring discomfort, and dealing with people who annoyed him. In these private notes he returns to the same difficulties, sometimes patiently, sometimes with the severity of someone tired of his own excuses. An emperor’s authority could make other people obey; it could not spare him the daily effort of governing his own temper and desires.
